oneLineAnswer: Alectinib is a prescription capsule for ALK-positive lung cancer, not a supplement for general use.
whatItIs: Alectinib is a prescription medicine taken by mouth as a capsule. Its brand name is Alecensa. Doctors group it with cancer drugs called kinase inhibitors. A kinase is an enzyme that switches other proteins on or off. It was first approved in the United States in 2015. It is approved only for lung cancers that test positive for a change in the ALK gene.
whatItDoes: Alectinib blocks the activity of two proteins, ALK and RET.
In laboratory studies it lowered the survival of tumour cells with abnormal ALK.
It also interrupted signals ALK sends inside cells, such as STAT3 and AKT.
The body turns part of it into M4, a breakdown product that acts in a similar way.
howPeopleUseIt: The label says to take the capsule with food and to swallow it whole.
After surgery for earlier disease, the label describes a planned course of about two years.
For cancer that has spread, treatment continues while it helps and is tolerated.
The label sets out steps for lowering the dose or stopping it if side effects are serious.
It is taken at home as a capsule rather than given as an injection.

commonSideEffects: Liver blood test changes were the most common problem in the pooled safety studies.
Constipation, tiredness, muscle aches, swelling, rash and cough each appeared in a fifth or more of treated patients.
Blood tests often showed raised creatine phosphokinase, an enzyme released by muscle.
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, headache, weight gain and taste changes were also reported.
Some people became sensitive to sunlight and were advised to use sunscreen.
seriousSigns: Severe liver injury, including drug-induced liver injury, occurred in some treated patients.
Lung inflammation, called interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis, occurred in 1.3% of patients in the pooled data.
Kidney problems occurred in 12% of patients, including severe cases, and a few were fatal.
A slow heart rate occurred in 11%; one fifth of monitored patients had post-dose rates below 50 beats per minute.
A red blood cell disorder called hemolytic anemia appeared in 3.1% of patients in one trial.
Very high blood triglycerides were reported after approval, sometimes with life-threatening pancreatitis.
whoShouldAvoid: People who are pregnant should not take it, because the label says it can harm a fetus.
Breastfeeding is stopped during treatment and for one week after the last dose.
Women who could become pregnant are advised to use effective contraception during treatment and for five weeks after.
Men with partners who could become pregnant are advised to use contraception for three months after treatment.
It is not for children; its safety and effectiveness in children have not been established.
The label lists no condition that rules out alectinib completely.

interactions: Alectinib is broken down by the liver enzyme CYP3A4, and the body then makes M4.
Studies found no meaningful change in alectinib levels when it was taken with posaconazole, rifampin or esomeprazole.
Lab tests suggested alectinib does not block CYP1A2, 2B6, 2C9, 2C19 or 2D6.
Lab tests also suggested alectinib and M4 can inhibit the transporters P-gp and BCRP.
A high-fat meal raised combined exposure to alectinib and M4 about threefold in one study.
pregnancyAndChildren: Alectinib can harm a fetus. The label says no data exist on its use in pregnant women, so the risk rests on animal studies. In animals, the drug caused fetal toxicity and abortion at doses that also harmed the mother. Women who could become pregnant are advised to use effective contraception during treatment and for five weeks after. Men with partners who could become pregnant are advised to use contraception for three months after. There are no data on alectinib in human milk. The label says not to breastfeed during treatment or for a week after. Its safety and effectiveness in children have not been established. Animal studies in young rats found changes in growing teeth and bone at higher exposures.
whatWeDoNotKnow: There are no human pregnancy data, so the fetal risk comes only from animal studies.
No study has measured how much alectinib passes into human breast milk.
No one has tested alectinib in children, so nothing is known about its effects there.
It has not been studied in people with severe kidney disease or end-stage kidney failure.
Carcinogenicity studies have not been done, and animal fertility studies have not been performed.
This record gives no numbers for how well alectinib works; the clinical studies sections were not reviewed.
The LiverTox review notes that the pattern of alectinib liver injury is still being described.

summary: This record covers what alectinib is, what it does in ALK-positive lung cancer, its common and serious side effects, its interactions, and its pregnancy and children cautions, drawing on the U.S. prescribing information plus PubChem and ClinicalTrials.gov.
